    Introduction

    Connecting to Falcon - SSH keys

    Instructor Note

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 25 minutes of live coding and 15 of exercises. Do the “before” demo first (type the password three times) so the gain is visible.

    Mixed audience. Demonstrate on your own system, but say aloud what is different on Windows (paths, no ssh-copy-id, agent service) and have a Windows machine or screenshots ready for PuTTY and MobaXterm. Ask PuTTY and MobaXterm users to follow the documentation page while you demonstrate the concepts.

    Common problems.

    • Nothing is shown while typing a passphrase, and people think the terminal is frozen.
    • Confusing the Falcon password with the key passphrase.
    • Windows: Notepad saves the config file as config.txt; the .ssh folder does not exist yet; paths use backslashes.
    • PuTTYgen: the Save public key button produces a format Falcon cannot read.
    • MobaXterm: its local terminal has a different home directory from Windows.
    • Someone sends or pastes the private key. Treat it as a teaching moment and have them regenerate the key.

    Fallback. The rest of the lesson does not depend on keys. If someone cannot get them working in the time, they can keep using their password and fix it afterwards with the documentation page or by contacting support.

    Finding the software and libraries you need

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 20 minutes of live coding and 15 of exercises. Let learners predict the result of each command before you run it. If time is short, drop the optional CPU-count challenge, which also fits the interactive sessions episode.

    Do not run sweep.py on the login node in the session. The os.cpu_count() check makes the point without loading the node. The actual effect is shown later on a compute node, with htop open next to the job.

    Check before the session.

    • Run every command on the node type used for the course and replace the illustrative outputs with the real ones. The Python and NumPy session at the start is from the login node.
    • Make sure there is something to find: a NumPy version from at least two toolchain generations, so the choosing challenge works. Adjust the matplotlib example to match what is installed.
    • Confirm that os.sched_getaffinity(0) inside a Slurm job shows the allocated CPUs on Falcon, because it depends on how Slurm’s CPU binding is configured.
    • If Falcon uses a spider cache, very recently installed software may not show up until it is refreshed, which can confuse a live demo.

    Software differs by architecture. The software trees on Falcon differ by CPU type, which you can see in the install paths (for example .../amd/zen4/... versus .../intel/cascadelake/...). The modules listed can therefore depend on the node you are on. This links to the architectures episode, and an optional extension is to run module spider numpy in an interactive session on a different node type and compare. Confirm that this matches how Falcon is configured before presenting it.

    Common problems.

    • Typing module load numpy and concluding that NumPy is missing.
    • Mixing toolchain generations, which produces errors that do not mention modules.
    • Piping module avail into grep without 2>&1.
    • Forgetting --login in a job script, so module: command not found.
    • Running a “quick test” of the real script on the login node.

    Estimating resources

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 25 minutes of live coding and 15 of exercises. Have learners type the script rather than paste it, and submit it all at about the same time. The training partition should keep the wait short, but check it beforehand.

    The resource values are deliberately generous. 16 GB is far more than this script needs, and 8 CPUs are far more than it can use. This sets up the efficiency episode, where seff shows the waste. Do not fix it now; say that we will come back to it.

    Check before the session.

    • Replace the illustrative outputs with the real ones, and the project and partition placeholders.
    • Run the script on a few different laptops, or have your own timings, so you know what to expect. A recent laptop with fast cores may beat a cluster core, which is good for the message but should not come as a surprise.
    • Confirm that the time, sysctl and PowerShell commands work on the machines learners will use.
    • The tab group syntax (tab) depends on your Workbench version. If it does not render, use three separate headings.

    Common problems.

    • Invalid account or account/partition combination specified: the project or partition is wrong or the learner does not belong to the project.
    • A script written or pasted in a Windows editor can contain Windows line breaks. Slurm then complains about DOS line breaks, or Bash reports a bad interpreter. Create or edit the file on Falcon, or convert it with dos2unix.
    • #SBATCH lines placed after a command are silently ignored.
    • module: command not found when --login is missing from the first line.
    • The job ends with TIMEOUT or OUT_OF_MEMORY when learners reduce the limits too far. Use it as a teaching moment.
    • Learners look in the .o file for errors instead of the .e file.
    • Someone runs python sweep.py 42 directly on the login node instead of submitting it. Remind them of the previous episode.

    Making the job script safe

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 25 minutes of live coding and 15 of exercises. The small echo and cd demonstrations run in a terminal on the login node and need no job, so they are safe and quick. Do them live and let learners predict each result first.

    Check before the session.

    • Replace the illustrative outputs, SCWFXXXXX, and the project and partition placeholders. Make sure each learner can create a directory under their scratch path.
    • Fill in the scratch policy and the quota command, and run the commands yourself first.
    • Check that module load works under set -u on Falcon. If a module prints an “unbound variable” error, use the set +u workaround from the callout.
    • Run the final script once and check that the scratch directory is removed.

    A useful extra demonstration. Introduce a deliberate typo (pyton sweep.py "${SEED}") and submit. Use sacct to show FAILED with exit code 127, and ls on scratch to show that the directory was kept. Then remove set -e and show the same job ending as COMPLETED even though no result exists. This is the best demonstration of why -e matters.

    This episode prepares later ones. OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK} is used in the scaling episode, where the CPU count is changed from the command line (sbatch -c 4 sweep-test.sh). The seed argument and unique names lead to array jobs, where SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID provides the seed.

    Common problems.

    • Windows line endings in a script written elsewhere (see the previous episode).
    • set -eu -pipefail copied from somewhere: it does not enable pipefail.
    • SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK: unbound variable because the script has no --cpus-per-task, which is set -u doing its job.
    • rm -rf guards: stress ${WORKDIR:?} and never deleting with wildcards.
    • Learners clean up scratch by hand before the job has finished.

    Can more cores make it faster?

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 25 minutes plus 15 of exercises. Submit the scaling jobs at the start of the episode, then explain the vocabulary and Amdahl’s law while they run, and come back to collect and plot the results.

    Capacity. If the whole class submits 64 or 128 CPU jobs at once, the training partition will fill up. The text limits learners to 32. Show the larger counts from your own measurements.

    Investigate the 128-CPU result before the session. The text deliberately lists possible causes rather than naming one, because the data does not settle it. Before teaching, it is worth running these:

    • Repeat 128 three times. Is it reproducible?
    • Record the node: sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,NodeList,Elapsed, and compare lscpu (model, sockets, threads per core) between the 64 and 128 CPU jobs.
    • Try 96, 112 and 127 CPUs. If 96 is fine and larger counts are slow, a processor boundary is likely. If 127 recovers, the cause is probably system activity on a fully allocated node.
    • Try -c 128 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=64, to separate “allocated 128” from “used 128 threads”.
    • Look at seff for the 128 CPU job. Threads that spin while waiting count as busy time, so the CPU efficiency may look high for a job that was very slow. This makes a good lead into the efficiency episode.

    Once you know the cause, update the “What happened at 128 CPUs?” section to say so.

    Check before the session.

    • Confirm that sbatch -c N overrides the #SBATCH line on Falcon and that SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK is set accordingly.
    • Make sure learners can run the plot: either matplotlib on their laptop, or have them paste the numbers into a spreadsheet.
    • Confirm the one-CPU run finishes comfortably inside the time limit (5 minutes in the script).

    Common problems.

    • Using -n instead of -c. The jobs run, but nothing changes.
    • Forgetting to change the result file name, so results overwrite each other or cannot be told apart.
    • Mixing up the script’s own time with Slurm’s Elapsed. Both are useful, but they differ by the start-up cost.
    • Reading the flattening curve as a “sweet spot”.
    • Windows line endings in the loop commands pasted from a document.

    Measuring efficiency with sacct and seff

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 25 minutes of teaching and 20 of exercises. The best use of time is the three seff reports side by side (1, 8 and 128 CPUs), then the “which job would you rather run?” challenge.

    Check before the session.

    • Run seff on your own 1, 8, 32, 64 and 128 CPU jobs and replace the illustrative numbers. The point of the section on high efficiency depends on the 128-CPU job really showing a high CPU efficiency and a much larger CPU Utilized than the single-CPU job. Confirm that on your data, and adjust the wording if it does not.
    • If you find the cause of the 128-CPU slowdown (see the previous episode), say so in that section and here.
    • Confirm that seff is available to learners, that the Cluster: line reads sensibly, and which memory values it reports for very short jobs. Run one of the small jobs and check MaxRSS.
    • Make sure the account and partition let learners see their own jobs with sacct without extra options.

    A useful comparison. If users can see their jobs in a web tool such as XDMoD, show the same jobs there as a “looking at many jobs” view. It makes the same point at the scale of a whole project.

    Common problems.

    • seff prints nothing or zeros for a job that has not finished. It reports only completed jobs.
    • Reading sacct times with a different format: Elapsed is HH:MM:SS, while TotalCPU can show fractions of a second or days (1-02:03:04).
    • Forgetting that MaxRSS is on the .batch line, so it does not appear with -X.
    • Treating a high CPU efficiency as proof that a job is healthy.
    • Right-sizing too aggressively: setting limits equal to the measurement, so the next run is killed.

    Watching a job run: interactive sessions, tmux, htop and ps

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 30 minutes of live coding and 15 of exercises. Do the setup together, step by step, because it is the part most likely to go wrong. The disconnection demonstration (close the window, reconnect, reattach) is the one learners remember.

    Check before the session.

    • Run the whole sequence on the node type learners will get. Confirm the exact srun command, that module works in the interactive shell (if it does not, start the shell with bash -l), and that htop, watch and pgrep are installed on the compute nodes.
    • Confirm that srun --jobid=<id> --overlap --pty bash works, and what happens without --overlap. In recent Slurm versions a second step may wait for the first to release the CPUs.
    • Check how long a run takes on the interactive CPUs, so that the burst is long enough to see in htop. With a few more CPUs the burst is shorter, and with fewer the serial part is a smaller share of the total.
    • Confirm that the number of R threads really jumps between 1 and the CPU count in the watch output. Spinning threads also show as R, so the picture can be less clean than the text suggests, and the discrepancy is itself worth showing.
    • Replace the illustrative outputs and add a real htop screenshot.
    • Ask learners to use at most 8 CPUs, and a short time limit, so that the interactive sessions leave room on the partition.

    Mixed audience. Windows users on PuTTY and MobaXterm need the terminal type set to xterm-256color for tmux and htop to display well. Selecting text with the mouse may need the Shift key while tmux mouse mode is on. The Ctrl+b prefix is the same on all systems. On a Mac, use the Control key, not Command.

    Common problems.

    • Starting srun before tmux, so that a lost connection ends the session.
    • Using tmux on falconlogin.cf.ac.uk, then not finding the session after reconnecting to the other login node.
    • Running htop in the second pane without attaching to the allocation, so it shows the login node.
    • Forgetting export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK} in the interactive shell, which changes the thread count.
    • Forgetting to exit the interactive session, so the allocation stays reserved until its time limit.
    • Reading the %CPU column of ps as a live figure.

    Finding the bottleneck with a profiler

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 15 minutes plus 10 for the exercise. Have the .map file ready for everyone in a shared location in case a learner cannot install the client, or the licence or version gets in the way. Show the client on the projector.

    The profile can change the story. Earlier episodes assumed that the long serial part of sweep.py is the pair-distance loop. That was inferred from the shape of the scaling curve and not measured. Look at the profile before the session, and if the time is split differently (for example if part of the serial time is in the eigenvalue calculation, which many linear algebra libraries do not parallelise well), update the earlier wording and the challenge solution above.

    Check before the session.

    • Run the job on the node type learners will use, and replace the summary and file name.
    • Check that --no-mpi is accepted by the installed version, and what the summary looks like without it.
    • Check the licence for the profiler on the compute nodes, and for the client on learners’ computers.
    • Make sure the .map file is copied out and not deleted by the cleanup.

    The matmul warning. Under MAP we saw RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in matmul for the covariance line, which we have not explained. Run the same job without map and check whether the warning is still there, and whether the results agree. Decide what to say if learners see it.

    Common problems.

    • Forgetting to load the profiler module, so map: command not found.
    • No .map file after the job, because the scratch directory was cleaned up.
    • A client older than the profiler cannot open the file.
    • The name of the file, with its date and time, makes it harder to find when many are in one directory.
    • Opening the profile on the cluster over X forwarding, which is slow. Use the client on your own computer.

    Improving the code

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 20 minutes plus 15 of exercises. Learners can submit the variants at the start and discuss while they run.

    Check before the session.

    • Fill in the table with your own numbers, and say which software versions differ between the two stacks.
    • Make sure the new stack exists for the node type learners will use, and that the script runs without changes there.
    • Confirm that the results match to the precision you expect, and decide what you will say if a learner’s differ.
    • Find out why the new stack is faster, if you can, by comparing the numpy and OpenBLAS versions, the kernel OpenBLAS chooses on the node, and the profiles. The text deliberately does not claim a reason.
    • If pdist gave no gain on your runs, look at the profile of that variant to see where the time went. It is a useful part of the story.

    Common problems.

    • Changing two things at once (the module and the code), so the effect cannot be attributed.
    • Comparing single runs. Timings vary from run to run, so repeat them.
    • Mixing modules from different toolchain generations after editing the module line.
    • Not saving the results with distinct names, so the old and new results overwrite each other (use the CPU count and job number as before).

    Running many analyses: array jobs and GNU Parallel

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 35 minutes of teaching and 25 of exercises. The array part and the QOS discussion take about half of it. The overhead and “which approach” discussions are the most valuable, so protect that time.

    Do not let the whole class hit the limit. If 20 learners each submit 100 tasks of 20 seconds, the class does to the scheduler exactly what this episode warns against. Options: demonstrate the 100-task submission once, from the instructor account; ask learners to submit it once, together, at a set time; or use a training QOS with a low limit so the effect is visible without the load. Warn the people who run the cluster before the session.

    Check before the session.

    • Find out what really happens on Falcon when 100 tasks are submitted with the training account: is the submission refused, or do tasks wait? Note the exact message or reason, and update the section on scaling up. Also check how the % throttle looks, and the value of MaxArraySize (scontrol show config | grep MaxArraySize).
    • Fill in the real limits and the contact address for limit requests.
    • Check the sacctmgr column names on your Slurm version.
    • Run both scripts end to end, and confirm the module name for GNU Parallel, and whether it prints a citation notice on first use (if so, mention that GNU Parallel asks to be cited in publications).
    • Confirm the memory figure: peak memory per task, from seff or MaxRSS, times the number of tasks at once.
    • Check how long 100 seeds take with 16 at a time, so the time limit in the script is realistic. Memory bandwidth shared between 16 tasks can make each one slower than a single run.
    • Confirm the job numbers of array tasks on Falcon and update the example outputs.

    A good demonstration of overhead. Submit 100 tasks as an array and the same 100 with GNU Parallel on the same number of CPUs, and compare the total time from submission to the last result. The array has to be scheduled task by task, and the difference is usually striking. The queue state of the cluster at that moment affects it, so try it first.

    Common problems.

    • The logs directory does not exist, so the log files are not written.
    • --mem set for one task in the Parallel script, and the job killed with OUT_OF_MEMORY.
    • Forgetting -j, so parallel starts more tasks than CPUs.
    • Forgetting the thread setting, and oversubscribing.
    • %10 mistaken for a limit on the number of tasks submitted. It limits only how many run at the same time.
    • Windows line endings in the scripts (see the earlier episodes).
    • Learners put --array in the script and also on the command line and wonder which wins. The command line does.

    Using GPUs

    Instructor notes

    Timing. About 20 minutes of teaching and 15 of exercises. This is the part that can be shortened if you are running late.

    What has and has not been tested. The kernel logic and the host code were checked in Numba’s CUDA simulator on a small case (the result agreed with SciPy), not on a real GPU. Run the whole sequence on a GPU node before the session.

    Check before the session.

    • Fill in the partition, --gres syntax and GPU types. Check whether the GPU partition ties CPUs or memory to GPUs, and adjust --cpus-per-task and --mem.
    • GPU nodes are scarce. Learners may queue for a long time. Consider a reservation for the session, or have a recorded run and its output ready so the lesson can continue.
    • Confirm module spider numba-cuda shows nothing on the login node, and the full name on the GPU node. Confirm the plain numba module does give the confusing error on your system if you plan to demonstrate it.
    • Confirm the driver on the GPU nodes supports the CUDA version in the module name.
    • Replace the illustrative outputs, and check the time for a larger m.
    • Make sure sweep-numba.py uses the same sizes as sweep.py (see make_data).

    Common problems.

    • Searching for the module on the login node and concluding it does not exist.
    • Loading numba instead of numba-cuda.
    • Forgetting --gres=gpu:1, so the job runs on a GPU node with no GPU visible, or in a CPU partition.
    • Leaving an interactive GPU session open, which holds a scarce resource.
    • Timing the first GPU call and reading the compilation time as the speed of the GPU.
    • A large m for the kernel with the naive access pattern can be slow. This is a demonstration of access, not of tuning.
